metadata.narrative: I’m on a small county health coalition in a mostly rural Appalachian area, and we just got a modest grant for diabetes work. We can’t do everything, so what should we put first: screening/prediabetes classes, diabetes self-management education, community health workers, food pantry partnerships, or built-environment/food access projects? How should we think about prevalence, rural access gaps, racial and income disparities, and what actually has evidence behind it, especially if our audience is county commissioners who want practical priorities and not just a list of programs?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A rural Appalachian county coalition working from a modest, one-time grant needs to sequence its diabetes investments by evidence strength, speed to impact, and fit with existing rural infrastructure rather than trying to run five programs at once.

Appalachian adults have a diagnosed diabetes prevalence near 12 percent, and diabetes mortality across the region runs about 11 percent higher than the national rate, rising to 33 percent higher in economically distressed counties.

People in distressed Appalachian counties also tend to be diagnosed two to three years earlier than their non-Appalachian peers, and a low-cost, coalition-based family education pilot across eleven Appalachian counties still produced measurable gains in knowledge and self-efficacy using modest resources.
Roughly a third of the federally defined "Diabetes Belt" lies in central and southern Appalachia, and West Virginia alone reports 15 percent diagnosed diabetes and another 35 percent prediabetes.

Residents of distressed Appalachian counties are 1.4 times more likely to have diabetes than residents of non-Appalachian counties, and prevalence among 45-to-64-year-olds runs roughly one in five in distressed counties versus one in eight elsewhere.

Nationally, diabetes is about 17 percent more common in rural than urban counties, and rural counties now carry the highest overall U.S. diabetes mortality rates, disparities most pronounced among men and in the South.

Racial disparities compound this rural burden: diagnosed diabetes runs about 15 percent among Black adults, 14 percent among American Indian/Alaska Native adults, and 12 percent among Hispanic adults, compared with 10 percent among White adults.

Income and education independently predict diabetes and foregone medical care, with lower-income, less-educated adults showing higher diabetes rates and higher rates of skipping care because of cost, especially in rural areas and the South.

These disparities are compounded by structural rural gaps: 62 percent of rural counties lack any diabetes self-management education program, rural hospitals are closing at an accelerating pace, and residents report less access to providers, insurance, transportation, and grocery stores.
Turning to the five options, the strongest, most transferable evidence supports community health workers as a rural-appropriate backbone strategy.

A Community Preventive Services Task Force review of 22 studies found community health worker interventions improve HbA1c, weight-related outcomes, and glycemic control among people at elevated diabetes risk.

A randomized trial among medically underserved Samoan villages found patients receiving home-visit community health worker support were twice as likely to achieve a clinically significant HbA1c improvement versus usual care.

Closer to home, a Mingo County, West Virginia community health worker program working with over 100 high-risk patients dropped average A1C from 10 percent to 7.5 percent within six months, while explicitly addressing food insecurity found during home visits.

Community health workers are inexpensive, can be hired locally, travel to patients rather than requiring travel, and can simultaneously screen, reinforce self-management, and connect households to food resources, making them a strong first priority.

Diabetes self-management education has deep cost-benefit evidence, showing every dollar spent yields $0.44 to $8.76 in net savings, with participants' costs running 5.7 to 14 percent lower than non-participants and a dose-response effect from repeated encounters.

A rural Virginia Cooperative Extension program delivering a four-week lifestyle curriculum produced a statistically significant A1C reduction among participants, showing the model can work through existing extension infrastructure rather than new clinical staff.

Because 62 percent of rural counties lack any self-management education program, this remains a strong second priority, particularly if layered onto an extension partnership or delivered via telehealth to control costs.

Screening and prediabetes classes built on the National Diabetes Prevention Program have excellent cost-effectiveness evidence, with one demonstration showing 37 percent of expected diabetes cases prevented over 15 years at $1,288 per quality-adjusted life year, and Medicare now reimbursing participation since 2018.

However, most of this financial payoff accrues to insurers and Medicare rather than the county budget, and standing up a brand-new CDC-recognized class requires enrollment volume and lead time a small rural grant may struggle to sustain, so funding referral and enrollment support into already-recognized programs is more efficient than building a new class.
Food pantry partnerships and produce-prescription approaches show solid, fast-to-launch clinical evidence.

A program pairing a health center with a food bank's choice pantries found diabetic patients making twelve or more pantry visits a year saw more than a one-point A1C drop, a clear dose-response signal.

A systematic review and NHANES-based microsimulation of produce-prescription programs projected A1C reductions of 0.63 percentage points and population-level savings exceeding $39 billion at scale, while the largest pooled evaluation to date, covering nine Wholesome Wave programs, found A1C down 0.3 points and blood pressure down 5 to 8 mmHg.

Because pantry partnerships can be added onto existing food bank relationships quickly and pair naturally with community health worker visits that already surface food insecurity, this is a reasonable third priority, especially bundled with the community health worker effort.
Built-environment and broader food-access projects have the weakest direct clinical evidence and the longest payback horizon.

A rigorous statistical comparison found that living in a food desert was not associated with diabetes control at all, and that individual-level income mattered far more than community-level food access, arguing for redirecting resources toward income-support programs rather than infrastructure alone.

Within the Appalachian coalition network, 96 percent of coalitions undertook built-environment projects like walking tracks compared with 75 percent pursuing food-access work, yet outcome data tied to built-environment investments were far thinner than data for community health workers, self-management education, or produce prescriptions.

For a one-time modest grant, built-environment work is best treated as a longer-term, separately-funded goal pursued through infrastructure grants rather than the coalition's first use of scarce dollars.

For commissioners wanting practical priorities rather than a program list: fund community health workers first because they multitask across screening, self-management support, and food-insecurity referral with the strongest rural outcome data; layer in a food pantry or produce-prescription partnership second because it is fast, cheap, and clinically proven; support self-management education third through an existing extension or telehealth partner; treat National DPP enrollment as a referral task rather than a new program; and hold built-environment infrastructure for future, separately funded grant cycles once initial data justify larger capital asks.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.
